title: TB3-06509
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the claimant), born XXXX XXXX XXXX 1990 is a citizen of Colombia who seeks refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1 DETERMINATION

The panel finds the claimant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that she would be personally subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture, or a risk to her life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment of punishment upon return to Colombia.

Details of the claimant's allegations can be found within the Basis of Claim (BOC) form2 and her testimony. To summarize, the claimant was a XXXX student volunteering at a clinic in the town of XXXX. On XXXX XXXX, 2012, while leaving the clinic she was stopped by a group of men, who identified themselves as FARC3 members, they insisted that she accompany them to a small house in the hills outside of the XXXX. She was instructed to provide XXXX care to an older gentleman who was complaining of XXXX XXXX. The claimant explained that she did not have the necessary tools to proceed; she was advised she could return to XXXX XXXX but the clinic was closed so she would have to wait and return the next day with the necessary tools. The men finally agreed, but took her student identification and she was taken back to the village and left with a threat that she must return or she would be killed. Her cousin lived in the same village, she made her way to his home and he having seen these men take her was able to aid her in leaving the village and returning home to XXXX. She made no reports to any authorities, including to the clinic or school, about the incident. She did not return to the clinic.

Two months went by with no contact, but while at XXXX XXXX some of her colleagues advised her that several patients were looking for her and had come to the University to seek her, asking for her by first and surname. Fearing it was the FARC seeking her she decided to flee the country. On XXXX XXXX, 2013, while waiting for her passport, FARC members arrived at her mother's home in XXXX. They asked for the claimant's whereabouts and when her mother denied knowing they left, giving her mother a warning that if her mother saw the claimant she should inform the claimant that FARC would find her eventually.

The University informed the claimant's mother they received a letter from the FARC. In XXXX 2013, threatening notes were left at the claimant's mother's house and at the same time the windows to the house had been vandalized. As a result, the claimant's mother and brother left the family home. The claimant at this time was residing with her father in the same city.

In XXXX 2013, the claimant's mother had been assaulted by members of the FARC, while leaving her employment. The FARC members demanded to know where the claimant was and gave her mother a warning that on the next occasion she would not be so fortunate.

The claimant obtained a visa for the U.S.A. and fled in XXXX 2013 but did not make a claim in the U.S.A. as she was informed as she was under a visitor visa she could not make a claim. The claimant's grandmother lives in Canada so she came to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2013 to submit a claim for refugee protection. Counsel's Submission
Counsel's submission is that the claimant's personal circumstances envelop both section 96 and 97 of the IRPA.

Counsel submissions as it relates to state protection is that the government of Colombia have been greatly hindered by endemic corruption, criminal elements and a grossly inefficient judicial system and public administration. The documentary evidence demonstrates that crime and corruption is permeated in the Colombian state apparatus and as a result undercuts the supposedly democratic nature of Colombian state institutions. Other adverse factors include FARC's power and influence as a criminal organization throughout Colombia, with its intrusion in to the political strife in Colombia has become closely tied with Colombia's domestic corruption and crime problems. Despite the Colombian authorities' protective steps, the government acknowledges its difficulties and inadequacies in tackling widespread crime, corruption and the influence of the criminal organizations. Counsel submits the claimant has sufficiently discharged her burden to demonstrate that adequate state protection is not or would not be available to her.4 ANALYSIS
The determinative issue in this claim is state protection. Identity

The claimant's identity as a citizen of Colombia is established by way of her testimonies, and the documentary evidence, namely the Colombian passport issued to the claimant.5 The panel is satisfied as to her identity as a citizen of Colombia.
The panel is satisfied that she graduated university under the XXXX program and is recognized as a XXXX in Colombia. Credibility

The panel does not agree with counsel that overall the claimant was a credible witness. The panel finds there were credibility issues fundamental to the allegations, which were not reasonably explained. The claimant did not persuade the panel she, on a balance of probabilities, was a generally credible and trustworthy witness. However; the determinative issue is state protection, and as such the issues of credibility of the claimant will be addressed within the analysis of state protection. State Protection

The panel does not agree with counsel as it relates to state protection in Colombia. The Board is not obliged to prove that Colombia can offer the claimant effective state protection; rather, the claimants bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that adequate state protection exists by adducing clear and convincing evidence that is reliable and probative, which satisfies the Board, on a balance of probabilities.6

The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has not discharged her burden or responsibility that adequate state protection is unavailable to her in Colombia. There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens except in situations where there is a complete breakdown.7 To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect that national.8 While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration, the test is whether the protection offered is adequate.9 The evidence that state protection is not adequate must be reliable and probative and it must also satisfy the panel, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.10

The documentary evidence shows that Colombia is a constitutional, multiparty democracy with a population of approximately 45 million. Colombia's most recent elections were considered free and fair. There are various security forces, reporting to civilian authorities with appropriate oversight. The Colombian National Police (CNP) is responsible for internal law enforcement and is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defense. The CNP shares law enforcement duties with the Prosecutor General's Corps of Technical Investigators (CTI). In addition to its responsibility to defend the country against external threats, the army shares limited responsibility for law enforcement and maintenance of order within the country. 11 Security forces report to civilian authorities though there are instances of them acting independently of their civilian control.12 The panel cannot agree with Counsel that Colombia have been greatly hindered by endemic corruption, criminal elements and a grossly inefficient judicial system and public administration The panel does not find that Colombia is in a state of breakdown.

The panel notes that there are problems with impunity of security forces, forced displacement, corruption, and societal discrimination. Impunity and an inefficient justice system subject to intimidation limited the state's ability to prosecute effectively individuals accused of human rights abuses and to bring to trial former members of paramilitary groups. The availability of drug-trafficking revenue often exacerbated corruption. Illegal armed groups--including the terrorist organizations Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and the National Liberation Army (ELN), as well as organized crime groups that contained some former paramilitary members--committed numerous abuses, including the following: political killings; killings of members of the public security forces and local officials; widespread use of land mines and improvised explosive devices (IEDs); kidnappings and forced disappearances; subornation and intimidation of judges, prosecutors, and witnesses; infringement on citizens' privacy rights; restrictions on freedom of movement; widespread recruitment and use of child soldiers; attacks against human rights activists; violence against women, including rape and forced abortions; and killings, harassment, and intimidation of teachers and trade unionists. Illegal armed groups continued to be responsible for most instances of forced displacement in the country.13

The panel has considered counsel's well-articulated submissions in regards to the state's inability to offer protection to its civilian due the scale of crime in Colombia and the resources of the FARC and other militants groups. However concerning the reach and influence of the FARC in Colombia today, the documentary evidence is mixed. Depending on who was consulted, the documentary evidence shows that the government counter-action has been increasingly successful and decisive and that the FARC is losing or has lost most of its key and powerful leaders, putting its central command apparatus in disarray. The government has had advertising campaigns to persuade FARC members to desert and reintegrate into civilian society.14 The panel concludes that Colombia, while not without significant challenges, is a functioning democracy and is not in a state of breakdown. However this serves only to set the framework of the panel's analysis of the claimant's particular circumstances Police

The panel notes the National Police has a force of approximately 4000 employees, this does not include the 3,000 employees of the Attorney General Office.15 The National Police of Colombia is comprised of the following directorates: Criminal Investigation and Interpol Directorate (Dirección Central de Policía Judicial) (Colombia n.d.c), which, under the direction of prosecutors and judges, cooperates in the investigation of crimes and in the detention of criminals (ibid. n.d.d). Intelligence Directorate (Dirección de Inteligencia de la Policía Nacional), which works in conjunction with other state intelligence services as well as with intelligence agencies from other countries to counteract criminal organizations with an international reach (ibid. n.d.e). Anti-kidnapping and Anti-extortion Directorate (Dirección de Antisecuestro y Antiextorsión de la Policía Nacional), the purpose of which is to develop action plans to [translation] "prevent, investigate, counteract and reduce kidnapping and extortion" (ibid. n.d.f). Mounted Police and Rural Security Directorate (Dirección de Carabineros y Seguridad Rural), the objective of which is to protect the [translation] "rural economic infrastructure" as well as natural parks and reserves, indigenous lands and border areas (ibid. n.d.g). This directorate develops inter-institutional plans in areas affected by criminal bands and identifies areas used by armed groups for criminal actions (ibid.). 16

The panel notes that the Colombian National Police (CNP) is responsible for internal law enforcement and is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defense. The CNP shares enforcement duties with the Prosecutor's General's Corps of Technical Investigations (CTI). In addition to its responsibility to defend the country against external threats, the army shares limited responsibility for law enforcement and maintenance of order within the country. For example, military units sometimes provided logistical support and security for criminal investigators to collect evidence in high-conflict or remote areas. The government continued to expand education and training of the armed forces in human rights and international humanitarian law.17

The perception of crime and corruption in Colombia is that it has worsened18 yet, the panel finds that the Colombian government has made serious and effective efforts to address corruption and crime, including increasing resources for the Prosecutor General's Office, to prosecute and punish officials, including members of the security services, who committed abuses, but some impunity still persisted. The primary government institution that investigates and prosecutes corruption is the Prosecutor General's Office, but Congress plays an investigative role in cases in which high government officials are involved. The Inspector General's Office investigates allegations of misconduct by public employees, including members of the state security forces. The Inspector General's Office referred all cases of human rights violations it received to the Prosecutor General Office's Human Rights Unit. As of October the Inspector General's Office had opened 207 disciplinary processes against members of the armed forces and police for human rights offenses and resolved 25 processes, including some from previous years. Of these, 15 resulted in judgments against the accused, and 10 resulted in acquittals. As of November the Prosecutor General's Office had obtained convictions of 543 accused members of the security forces. During the first 10 months of the year, the prosecutor general won convictions against 70 members of the security forces accused of extrajudicial killings, including two majors, three captains, four lieutenants, five sub-lieutenants, eight sergeants, seven corporals, and 41 lower-ranking soldiers.19

Dozens of convictions were obtained in cases transferred to civilian courts, but far more cases proceeded slowly due to a shortage of prosecutors and delaying tactics by defense lawyers.20 Furthermore, a special investigative unit of the Supreme Court of Justice, which examined members of congress and senior government officials, reported that during the year the unit opened investigations involving 113 sitting or former senators, resulting in two acquittals, nine convictions, and 101 cases closed for lack of evidence, with one case closed for having exceeded the statute of limitations. In addition the unit opened investigations involving 180 current or former members of congress, resulting in six convictions, 171 cases closed for lack of evidence, and three cases closed for having exceeded the statute of limitations. The unit also opened investigations involving five current or former governors, resulting in two convictions, one case closed for lack of evidence, and two cases closed for having exceeded the statute of limitations. Under laws 600 and 906, the Prosecutor General's Office investigated inspectors, comptrollers, and other high officials. At year's end the prosecutor general had a total of 1,393 cases registered under the two laws. The majority of these cases were under investigation or in preliminary stages of prosecution, but 12 had gone to trial by year's end. Thus, the panel finds that the authorities have taken direct action to address crime and corruption.

The Prosecutor General's Office is responsible for investigations and prosecutions of criminal offenses. Its Human Rights Unit, which includes 13 satellite offices, specializes in investigating human rights crimes, and its 126 specialized prosecutors were handling 6,320 active cases at the end of October. The panel notes that there are various agencies in Colombia that deal with complaints as they relate to the armed groups. According to the website of the National Police of Colombia (Policía Nacional de Colombia), that institution, the Administrative Department of Security (Departamento Administrativo de Seguridad, DAS) and the Corps of Technical Investigators (Cuerpo Técnico de Investigación, CTI) of the Office of the Attorney General (Fiscalía General de la Nación) are the agencies responsible for receiving complaints of crimes such as homicide, bodily injuries, threats, sexual violence and harassment, trafficking in persons, theft, fraud, counterfeiting, extortion, terrorism and kidnapping (Colombia n.d.a). The US Department of State indicates in its Country Reports on Human Rights Practices for 2010 that "the National Police are responsible for internal law enforcement and are under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defense" (US 8 Apr. 2011 Sec. 1d). The report also indicates that law enforcement duties are shared with the DAS and the CTI (ibid.). However, the DAS website indicates that the department is being disbanded and will conclude all operations in 2013 (Colombia n.d.b).21

DAS has been disbanded and in an October 2011 decree which dismantled the DAS and created the National Intelligence Directorate (NID), this new agency is responsible for intelligence but does not have arrest authority. As of October the NID had contracted 206 of the 599 employees it planned to hire. Of these, 17 were former DAS officials.22

The panel notes that collaboration between security forces and illegal armed groups declined following AUC demobilization, but rights groups report toleration of the roughly 8,000-strong paramilitary successor groups in some regions. Primary responsibility for combating them rests with the police, who lack the resources of the military, are frequently accused of colluding with criminal groups, and are largely absent from many rural areas where the groups are active. However, several of the paramilitary groups' key leaders were killed or arrested in 2012, as were several of Colombia's most wanted drug traffickers.23

The panel finds that over the past ten years, Colombia has developed a strong institutional capacity to combat drug trafficking, which is often controlled and financed by the FARC and ELN (both designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations), as well as BACRIM and other narcotics trafficking organizations. These groups all use drug cultivation and trafficking proceeds to expand their influence and control and fund attacks on security forces. In response, the Colombian government launched the National Consolidation Plan (PNC) in 2009 to focus coordinated government efforts on selected areas where violence and drug trafficking converged. Following a strategic review, the effort was re-launched in 2011 as the National Plan for Territorial Consolidation (PNCT) and authorities created the Administrative Unit for Territorial Consolidation (UACT) in January 2012 to coordinate the activities of government institutions in these areas. Much of 2012 was spent staffing and establishing the administrative, legal, and contractual guidelines for the unit's operation. Judicial impunity reportedly declined in 2012, though serious challenges remain. Most cases are resolved through plea agreements, and a modest number through trials.24

As it relates to corruption, the panel notes there are positive actions taken by the Colombian authorities that have led to positive results which include arrests and convictions of those involved in corruption. There is nothing before the panel to suggest the state was involved in the threats, or that the state would refuse to investigate any allegations of threats by FARC. The documentary evidence shows that the government counter-action has been increasingly successful and decisive when dealing with both criminals and the legendary FARC.25

The panel has considered the number of articles submitted by counsel as it relates to the FARC, noting some of the articles are dated.26 The panel prefers to the most recent evidence in the evidence including the National Documentation Package that finds that there have been gains and initiatives that show that the government is addressing the problems of not only FARC but other criminal organizations as well, and not just at the legislative level but also at the operational level.27 The Board accepts that Colombia is experiencing challenges in addressing the criminality and corruption that exist within the country with duelling priorities of trying to reach a peace accord with the militant groups such as FARC and the need to address the criminal elements that exists in Colombia. Yet, there has been evidence of some success in addressing these problems, Guerrilla group members continued to demobilize. At the end of October, according to the Ministry of Defense, 840 members of guerrilla groups had demobilized, compared with approximately 1,300 during the same period in 2011, a 36 percent reduction in demobilizations. The Organization of American States (OAS) verified all stages of demobilization and reintegration into society of former combatants from the guerrilla and paramilitary groups.28 Courts convicted some FARC members for kidnappings. For example, on November 27, Alberto Caceres Macon (El Piloso) received a sentence of 40 years for crimes including the 1999 kidnapping and subsequent murder of foreign nationals Terence Freitas, Ingrid Washinowatok, and Larry Gay Lahe, who had been working to organize indigenous groups.29

The government took significant steps to increase resources for the Prosecutor General's Office.30 Primary responsibility for combating crime rests with the police, who lack the resources of the military, are frequently accused of colluding with criminal groups, and are largely absent from many rural areas where the groups are active. However, several of the paramilitary groups' key leaders were killed or arrested in 2012, as were several of Colombia's most wanted drug traffickers.31

The panel notes the documentary evidence shows that the government counter-action has been increasingly successful and decisive, including in 2012 a dramatic drop in the murder rate in Colombia though some areas remain besieged by violence.32 The panel notes that the FARC is losing or has lost most of its key and powerful leaders, putting its central command apparatus in disarray. The government has had advertising campaigns to persuade FARC members to desert and reintegrate into civilian society.33

The documentary evidence shows that the government of Colombia has had success in recent years in weakening the FARC. Government has undertaken to increase the security forces providing proactive security and ensuring that the FARC actions are either stopped or limited. The defence forces have been achieving tangible results against the guerrillas with significant backing by the U.S. and other western governments.

Other indicator of the state's continuing efforts to address the conflict with FARC include but is not limited to34: On 10 October 2011, AFP reports that [translation] "at least" 11 FARC guerrillas from Front 33 were killed in a police operation in the department of Norte de Santander. In February 2012, Caracol Radio, a radio station based in Bogota, reported the killing of the commander of Front 62 in the department of Meta (14 Feb. 2012). This front was responsible for coordinating the FARC's eastern and southern blocs (Caracol Radio 14 Feb. 2012.). One month later, Colombia Reports, a Medellin-based, English-language news source (n.d.), reported the detention of four guerrillas from Front 34 in the department of Chocó (6 Mar. 2012).35 [...] Police captured FARC's plans for its mobile column Ismael Ayala to attack police stations in the Bogota neighbourhoods of Arborizadora Alta, Candelaria and San Francisco (El Espectador 11 Oct. 2011). Sources report that the National Police also detained 12 FARC guerrillas accused of committing [translation] "various" attacks in Bogota and the central zone of Colombia (AP 29 Feb. 2012; NOTIMEX 28 Feb. 2012), as well as manufacturing security force uniforms in order to install roadblocks and mount attacks against military targets and civilians (ibid.). Also, El Espectador reports the discovery by the police of [translation] "'clandestine hospitals'" belonging to the FARC in a neighbourhood in south Bogota and in the department of Meta (3 Mar. 2012). The hospitals were used for injured guerrillas (El Espectador 3 Mar. 2012). In another government operation, agents of the Office of the Attorney General (Fiscalía General de la Nación) seized 80 mortar shells and a tripod just outside of Bogota; the weapons belonged to FARC urban militias (NOTIMEX 19 Mar. 2011).36 [...] In Santiago de Cali, the army seized 213 improvised explosive devices belonging to the mobile column Gabriel Galvis in a rural area outside the city (El Espectador 26 May 2011). El Espectador reported that the Metropolitan Police of Cali seized 100 bars of explosives belonging to the FARC that allegedly would have been used for attacks in the city (27 Sept. 2011). Bogota-based Radio Santa Fe also reports the seizure in Santiago de Cali of two [translation] "high-power rifles" and 100 grenades that were allegedly intended for the FARC in southern Colombia (30 Jan. 2012).37 Over the past ten years, Colombia has developed a strong institutional capacity to combat drug trafficking, which is often controlled and financed by the FARC and ELN (both designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations), as well as BACRIM and other narcotics trafficking organizations. These groups all use drug cultivation and trafficking proceeds to expand their influence and control and fund attacks on security forces.38 Guerrilla group members continued to demobilize. As of the end of August, according to the Ministry of Defense, 917 members of guerrilla groups had demobilized, compared with approximately 840 during the same period in 2012, an 8 percent increase in demobilizations. The Organization of American States (OAS) verified all stages of demobilization and reintegration into society of former combatants from the guerrilla and former paramilitary groups. 39 Implementation of the 2005 Justice and Peace Law (JPL) continued. The Justice and Peace Unit in the Prosecutor General's Office is responsible for the required investigation and prosecution of demobilized persons, and an interagency commission on justice and peace coordinates its implementation. Participants in the justice and peace process could receive reduced sentences if they complied with the terms of the JPL. Testimony from voluntary confessions also triggered investigations of politicians, military members, major agricultural producers, and government officials' past ties to paramilitary forces. Some of the investigations resulted in prosecutions and convictions.40 As of July, 4,151 former paramilitary and guerrilla defendants (postulados) had participated in confession hearings (versiones libres). During these sessions the postulados confessed to 42,309 crimes, and information was obtained that resulted in the exhumation of 5,301 victims. As of May, 1,126 postulados had been initially charged, and 680 of these had been formally charged in presentations before the courts by the Prosecutor General's Office's Justice and Peace Unit. Postulados who do not fully comply by confessing crimes, turning over illegally acquired assets, and ceasing their criminal activity are moved for expulsion from the JPL process by the Prosecutor General's Justice and Peace Unit. As of July the Justice and Peace Unit prosecutors had filed for the expulsion of 88 postulados before the Justice and Peace courts.41 Courts convicted some FARC members for kidnappings. Through October the unit to combat kidnapping and extortion at the Prosecutor General's Office reported 13 convictions during the year for kidnappings committed by the FARC, while the Human Rights Unit reported 61 such convictions in the same period. For example, on March 21, the second specialized criminal judge of Antioquia sentenced Luis Norbey Caicedo Correa (alias Esneider or Manchas), head of the FARC mobile column Jacobo Arenas, to 51 years' imprisonment for the 2007 kidnappings of Juan David Arango Velez and Sergio Jaramillo Arriola.42

Though mixed, the panel finds that the authorities in Colombia are addressing at an operational level the guerrillas, drug and organized crime problems it has due to the many years of conflict.43 The panel acknowledges that there are instances where the security forces, including the police, act independent of civilian control, though much less frequently than in past years. However, weighed against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that Colombia candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the corruption and impunity that exists. The government continued efforts to improve respect for human rights and prosecute and punish officials, including members of the security services, who committed abuses, but some impunity persisted. The panel recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence as it relates to the successes of the Colombian authorities, however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is an adequate state protection in Colombia for victims of crime, that Colombia is making serious efforts to address the problem of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims.

A claimant must approach the state for protection, providing that state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.44 In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim. Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that it is not always successful at doing so will not rebut the presumption of state protection.45 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.46 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.47

In view of the evidence before me, the panel finds the claimant has not provided the requisite clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in Colombia is inadequate, since the claimant has not shown she has taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances particular to herself to seek protection before seeking international protection.

The panel has credibility concerns as it relates to the incident of XXXX 2012. The claimant was seized by unknown men who identified themselves as FARC members while leaving the XXXX clinic, taken to another location, but released as she didn't have the tools to do XXXX. After her release she did not contact the clinic to explain what happened, she just left. She did not contact the University to advise them what happened nor to advise that FARC members had her student identity card. The panel does not find this credible. When asked why she failed to do this she testified she did not want anyone to have access to her. She also testified she did not inform the school as they would demand she go to the police. The panel does not find it credible particularly in light that she testified that members of FARC had her student identity card.

The claimant testified that her mother continues to be targeted by the FARC as the guerrillas continue to seek the claimant, yet there was no information provided by the claimant's mother to support this allegation, though her mother did in fact send the documents obtained to the claimant including the affidavit from the claimant's cousin who states he witnessed the claimant being taken by the FARC.48 The panel does not find it credible that the claimant's mother would forward all these documents yet not make any statement as it relates to FARC continued seeking of the claimant.

The claimant was asked why she didn't inform the XXXX clinic that there were FARC men looking for XXXX aid; she testified she didn't think of it. In the claimant's particular situation she did not approach the police or the Attorney General's office to file a denunciation. When asked why she failed to approach either, she stated her father told her that it was not a good idea, that information that is provided to the police is tantamount to giving information to the FARC. Colombia's efforts to eliminate the FARC are indicated within the documentary evidence. The assertion of the claimant that the police do not offer adequate protection is unsubstantiated. The police were not given the opportunity to offer protection, instead the claimants left the area and then the country. This is not indicative of the police unwillingness to offer protection. The panel finds the claimant has not tested whether the state was able or willing to provide protection. The panel notes the claimant moved to her father's address and was not contacted again directly.

The panel considered all the evidence, including contrary evidence relied upon by the claimant, and has found that the preponderance of the objective evidence indicates that adequate state protection is available. The panel has considered the claimant's personal profile, a young professional woman targeted by the FARC, the panel does not find that in the circumstances particular to the claimant, that she would not be able to access adequate state protection if she so sought it from the Colombian government. Based on the claimant's profile and the situation of the FARC in Colombia, the panel finds the FARC as an organization would not consider the claimant as a high-value target.49 There is nothing in her profile to suggest that the authorities would be unwilling or unable to offer her adequate state protection.

The panel, having considered the totality of the evidence, including counsel's submissions, finds the claimant, in the circumstances particular to this case, has failed to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection with clear and convincing evidence. The panel is therefore not persuaded that Colombia would not be reasonably forthcoming with adequate state protection should the claimant wish to seek and pursue it.

For all these reasons, the panel determines the claimant is not Convention refugee or persons in need of protection, whether under section 96 or 97 of the IRPA. The panel rejects this claim.
